title: Notes on the principal bundle and the associated bundle
content:
Given a base manifold \(M\), and a
group action: \(G\) acts on vector
space \(V\) (which induces a
representation of \(G\) using \(\mathrm{GL}(V)\)), we define 2 related
fibre bundles, one is the principal bundle, intuitively just like \(M \times G\) (locally and trivially), and
the other one is the associated bundle, intuitively just like \(M \times G \times V\), however factored by
a two-side equivalent relation: \((m, gh, v)
\sim (m, g, hv)\). We will make our intuition rigorous as in the
following way.
Now we will make our language rigorous. Firstly we define what is a
fibre bundle. A fibre bundle is a 4-tuple \((P, π, M, F)\), where \(π: P \twoheadrightarrow M\) is a surjective
mapping from the total space \(P\) to
the base manifold \(M\), and at each
point \(m \in M\), there is \(\pi^{-1}(m) \cong F\), and here the
isomorphism \(\cong\) can be understood
in various way, depending on the context. If we want \(F\) to be a group here, then \(P\) should have both the topological
structure as being a manifold and the algebraic structure as having a
group multiplication at every point of the base manifold. Then we
consider what a principal bundle is. We consider a fibre bundle \(π: P \twoheadrightarrow M\), where the
fibre F is a group. (Or more precisely, the torsor of the group ——the
group itself but just forgetting the 1) Now we define a right action of
the group \(G\) onto the fibre bundle
\(P\), just defined locally as: \(p \in P, p ``='' (m, g)\), and
\(h \in G\), the right action \(R_h\) maps \(p\) to \((m,
gh)\), i.e. \(R_h(p) = R_h( (m, g) ) =
(m, g) \cdot h = (m, gh)\). We call this structure a principal
bundle.
So we know, a principal bundle consists of 2 basic ingredients: the
base manifold \(M\) and the
corresponding group \(G\). We can
define various principal bundle on a manifold \(M\), and switch between them by choosing
different group \(G\). Each choice of
the group \(G\) may cause different
properties of the principal bundle, and be interested by researchers in
different area. For example, if we choose \(G
= U(1)\), which is the group of all unit complex numbers in \(\mathbb{C}\), then we can define the \(U(1)\)-bundle on \(M\). Now we introduce the concept of the
associated bundle, with respect to \(G\), on the manifold \(M\). First, to define an associated bundle
on M, we need to select an arbitrary group action \(G \times V \rightarrow V\) (which is
exactly a representation of \(G\) using
\(\mathrm{GL}(V)\)), where \(V\) is a vector space, and \(G\) acts on \(V\) just like a matrix. Now we define 2
different fibre bundles, one is the principal bundle, \(\pi: P\twoheadrightarrow M\) (elements are
typically written as \((m, g)\)), and
locally \(\pi^{-1}(m) \cong G\), and
the other one is the associated bundle, defined as a quotient space, of
the direct product \(P \times V\)
(elements are typically written as \(((m, g),
v))\), divided by the equivalent relation \(\sim: ((m, gh), v) \sim ((m, g), hv)\).
So we find that the associated bundle is an object that somewhat
consists of all the triples \((m, g,
v)\), where the first item \(m\)
is the selected point on the base manifold \(M\), and the group element \(g\) represents for the chosen gauge at the
point \(m\), which is an element of the
gauge transformation group, and so it is in \(G\), then finally the vector \(v\) is what we are actually interested in.
The vector \(v\) is the main element we
are considered about at the point m of the manifold \(M\), but however due to the gauge
invariance property of some physical models, it can not be uniquely
determined since some gauge transformation can be conducted.
In conclusion, the concept of an associated bundle is closely related
to the concept of its principal bundle. If we only care about the
principal bundle, then this is somehow lacking of meaning since we don’t
know whom is to be acted on using the given principal bundle. So if we
say “\(M \times G\)” is a principal
bundle, we are supposing that some vector space \(V\) is prepared to be acted by the group
\(G\) and principal bundle is just like
the one who acts on the other fibre bundles.
Now we go further to consider some concrete examples in physical
application. We consider the quantum mechanics, in which a wave function
is equivalent to what obtained by a phase shift to itself. We consider
the principal bundle, chosen as the \(U(1)\)-bundle on the base manifold \(M\), and the bundle of all wave functions
(scalar field): \(M \times \mathbb{C}
\twoheadrightarrow M\) is whom to be acted on. We select \(B = (M \times U(1)) \times \mathbb{C} /
\sim\) as the associated bundle. Now every section of \(B\) is a field on \([M \times U(1)] = \{(m, g) \cdot h | h \in G \} =
\{(m, gh) | gh \cdot G\} \cong M\); at each point “\(m\)” we assigned a “vector” \(v\), where \(v\) is actually a set that consists of all
pairs of \((\text{gauge},
\text{vector})\): “\(v =\)”
\({(g, v) | g \in G}\), in a way that
given every gauge at point m there is a vector \(v\) (in ordinary sense) and all these pairs
compatible with each other. Note that gauge is placed between the point
\(m\) and the vector \(v\), so \((m, g,
v)\) for the triple. For our quantum mechanics example, \(m\) is in the manifold \(M\), \(g\)
is in \(U(1)\), and \(v\) is in \(\mathbb{C}\).
